title: As ... As: Things and Situations
why: These similes describe objects, tasks and situations with colour: how easy, obvious, old or safe. Several are regional, so knowing who says what helps you sound natural in Canada, the US or Britain.
know: British: safe as houses, cheap as chips
understand: literal to abstract: cold as ice, dead as a doornail
able: describe tasks, objects, evidence and health with natural similes
use the casual form without the first as, and the about as ... as pattern
recognise the history behind dead as a doornail in Shakespeare and Dickens
mistakes: Her hands were as cold as snow.
As cold as ice. Snow is understandable but it isn't the fixed simile.
Don't worry, the recipe is as easy as cake.
As easy as pie, or a piece of cake. Don't mix the two.
After a week in bed I feel right like rain.
I feel as right as rain (or right as rain). Never like in this simile.
Your money is safe like houses in a Canadian bank.
Safe as houses, and it's British. In Canada, perfectly safe or as safe as can be is more natural.
The proof is clear as the day.
Clear as day, with no article. You can also say as plain as day.
bigidea: With things and situations, as ... as similes mostly work as strong intensifiers. As easy as pie simply means very easy; as old as the hills means extremely old. The image is memorable, but nobody thinks about pies or hills.

Some of these similes have travelled from the physical to the abstract. A doornail is literally a lump of iron, but a project, a law or a marriage can be as dead as a doornail. Cold as ice describes your hands, but also an unfriendly person.
Irony is common: as clear as mud means confusing, and about as useful as a chocolate teapot (British) means useless. Listen for the tone of voice: the same frame can praise or mock.
hidden: Thanks for the instructions. They're as clear as mud.
The lake was like glass at six in the morning.
Turn on the fan; this room is like an oven.
The highway across the prairies is as straight as an arrow.
The house was as quiet as a tomb after the guests left.
Leave the bread out overnight and it'll be as hard as a rock.
The new software runs like a dream.

expressions.example: The new carbon-fibre bike is as light as a feather.
expressions.bend: Often light as a feather. Also feather-light and light as air (for food: the soufflé was light as air).
expressions.note: Can describe a person being carried, or a feeling of relief. Not as light as a plume.

expressions.meaning: very cold; also emotionally cold and unfriendly
expressions.example: The cottage was as cold as ice when we arrived in January.
expressions.bend: Ice-cold as an adjective (an ice-cold drink). For people: she was cold as ice to him.
expressions.note: Common wrong version: as cold as snow. For drinks, ice-cold is positive; for people, cold as ice is negative.

expressions.meaning: extremely old; very well known for a long time
expressions.example: That excuse is as old as the hills; teachers have heard it for decades.
expressions.bend: Usually about ideas, jokes, tricks or problems. Also as old as time, which is more poetic.
expressions.note: Saying a person is as old as the hills is teasing and can offend. For people, use it only about yourself.

expressions.meaning: completely obvious or easy to see
expressions.example: From the security video it was as clear as day who had taken the parcel.
expressions.bend: Also as plain as day. No article before day. Crystal clear is more about being easy to understand.
expressions.note: Opposite, ironic: as clear as mud. Don't say clear as the day.

expressions.example: Once you know the shortcut, the tax form is as easy as pie.
expressions.bend: Easy as pie is most common. Near-synonyms: a piece of cake, easy as ABC, easy peasy (childish or playful).
expressions.note: Mainly North American but understood everywhere. Don't mix it into as easy as cake.

pic.label: a doornail (a big nail hammered into an old door)

expressions.meaning: completely dead; also completely finished or failed
expressions.example: After the vote, the pipeline proposal was as dead as a doornail.
expressions.bend: Used for plans, deals, batteries and phones as well as people and animals. Often dead as a doornail.
expressions.note: Recorded since the 1300s. For something extinct or out of date, as dead as a dodo is better.

expressions.meaning: perfectly healthy or fine again, especially after illness
expressions.example: Drink plenty of fluids and you'll be as right as rain by Monday.
expressions.bend: Almost always be/feel/look right as rain, often in the future: you'll be right as rain. Fixed: no like.
expressions.note: Originally British, common in Canada, slightly old-fashioned and reassuring. Said by doctors, parents and grandparents.

expressions.meaning: very safe or secure, with no risk
expressions.example: Her parents told her a government bond was as safe as houses.
expressions.bend: British; rare in North America. Fixed plural houses. Often ironic since housing crashes.
expressions.note: Canadians and Americans would say perfectly safe, a safe bet or rock-solid.

culture.how: Dickens opens the story by insisting that Scrooge's partner Marley is as dead as a doornail. The narrator then jokes that he can't see why a doornail is especially dead, and would prefer a coffin nail, but won't argue with his ancestors' wisdom.
culture.ask: Why do you think Dickens starts a ghost story by insisting so strongly that someone is dead?
culture.find: Dickens A Christmas Carol opening Marley dead as a doornail

culture.how: The rebel leader Jack Cade, hungry and hiding in a garden, threatens to leave its owner as dead as a doornail. Shakespeare didn't invent the simile, which was already centuries old, but he shows how common it was in everyday speech.
culture.ask: Which similes in your language are hundreds of years old? Do people still use them?
culture.find: Shakespeare Henry VI Part 2 Jack Cade doornail

culture.work: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
culture.how: When the wind dies, the mariner's ship is stuck for days on a flat, motionless ocean. Coleridge compares it to a painted ship on a painted sea: as still and lifeless as a picture. The as ... as frame makes the stillness feel unbearable.
culture.ask: Describe a moment in your life when everything seemed to stop, using an as ... as simile.
culture.find: Coleridge Rime of the Ancient Mariner painted ship painted ocean

culture.how: The title simile is the whole message: the singer accuses someone of being cold as ice, emotionally hard and willing to hurt others to get what she wants, and warns that she'll regret it. It shows the simile moving from temperature to personality.
culture.ask: Is calling someone cold as ice worse than calling them unfriendly? What does the image add?

match.why: Physical or emotional cold. Not as cold as snow.
Often about jokes, excuses and tricks.
As obvious as daylight. Opposite, ironic: as clear as mud.
Casual. Close to a piece of cake.
Used since the 1300s, by Shakespeare and by Dickens.
British. North Americans say perfectly safe or a safe bet.

sort.h: Sort the similes: are they about something easy or obvious, something old, dead or finished, or a physical quality?

items.w: as plain as the nose on your face
items.why: So obvious that everyone should see it.
As easy as learning the alphabet.
Extinct or totally out of date. The dodo bird died out in the 1600s.
Poetic: as old as anything can be.

pick.q: My granddaughter carried the suitcase upstairs easily; it was ___.
pick.why: Very light in weight = as light as a feather.

pick.q: The furnace broke overnight and by morning the kitchen floor was ___.
pick.why: Very cold = as cold as ice.

pick.q: Blaming the dog for missing homework? That excuse is ___.
pick.why: Very old and familiar = as old as the hills.

pick.q: Once you look at the numbers, it's ___ that the store is losing money.
pick.why: Completely obvious = as clear as day.

pick.q: Changing the printer cartridge is ___; I'll show you.
pick.why: Very easy = as easy as pie.

pick.q: After the senator retired, the bill she'd championed was ___.
pick.why: Completely finished = as dead as a doornail.

pick.q: It's just a sprained wrist. In a couple of weeks you'll be ___.
pick.why: Fine again after injury = as right as rain.

pick.q: In 1990s Britain, many people believed property was ___.
pick.why: Completely secure = as safe as houses (British).

spot.q: The wind off the lake was as cold as snow this morning.
spot.why: The fixed simile is cold as ice.

spot.q: Assembling this bookshelf is as easy as cake.
spot.why: As easy as pie, or a piece of cake. Don't blend them.

spot.q: The motive was as clear as the day once we read her emails.
spot.why: No article: clear as day, plain as day.

spot.q: My phone fell in the lake and now it's as dead as a door.
Take this medicine and you'll be right like rain in no time.
spot.why: Right as rain, with as and no article.

type.q: The pastry was as light as a ___; you've outdone yourself.
type.why: As light as a feather: very light.

type.q: Her voice was as cold as ___ when she answered the reporter.
type.why: As cold as ice: unfriendly and hard.

type.q: That joke is as old as the ___; my grandfather told it.
type.why: As old as the hills: very old. Always plural hills.

type.q: It was clear as ___ that he hadn't read the report.
The deal's as dead as a ___ now that the buyer has pulled out.
type.why: As dead as a doornail: completely finished.

type.q: In London people used to say bricks and mortar were as safe as ___.
type.why: As safe as houses: completely secure. British.

bend.q: A colleague is giving confusing directions. Which ironic reply sounds natural? ___
opts: Thanks, that's as clear as mud.
Thanks, that's as clear as day mud.
Thanks, that's as muddy as clear.
bend.why: As clear as mud is the ironic opposite of as clear as day.

bend.q: A Canadian doctor is reassuring a patient. Which version sounds most natural? ___
opts: You'll be right as rain by the weekend.
You'll be as right like rain by the weekend.
You'll be right as the rains by the weekend.
bend.why: Dropping the first as is natural in speech. The rest is fixed.

bend.q: Which version describes cold drinks naturally? ___
bend.why: Ice-cold is the adjective form, positive for drinks.

bend.q: Which version uses the ironic about as ... as pattern naturally about a useless gadget? ___
opts: It's about as useful as a chocolate teapot.
It's about as useful like a chocolate teapot.
It's about useful as a chocolate teapot.
bend.why: About as ... as is often ironic. Chocolate teapot is a British joke image: useless.

talk: Dickens begins a ghost story by joking about doornails. Why might a writer use a funny, old simile at a serious moment?
Coleridge compares a stuck ship to a painting. Describe a time when you felt stuck, using one simile from this lesson and one of your own.
Role-play: you're a doctor or pharmacist reassuring a nervous patient. Use right as rain and as easy as pie naturally.
Which of today's similes would you avoid in a business email, and which would be fine? Explain your choices.
Is anything really as safe as houses today? Talk about housing, savings or jobs in your country.

match.why: Used for land, tires and also for flat jokes or events.
Usually about people: strong, unemotional, hard to hurt.
British. Chips are fries, a cheap snack.
Often after a repair: the car's as good as new.

match.l: as plain as the nose on your face
match.why: Something everyone can see. Close to as clear as day.
The opposite of what the words seem to say.

pick.q: Saskatchewan is famous for being ___, so you can see storms coming for hours.
pick.why: Completely flat = as flat as a pancake.

pick.q: Our old sergeant was ___, but she was always fair.
pick.why: Tough and unsentimental = as hard as nails.

pick.q: In Leeds you can get a full breakfast that's ___.
pick.why: Very cheap = as cheap as chips (British).

pick.q: The jeweller fixed the clasp, and Grandma's necklace looks ___.
pick.why: Repaired perfectly = as good as new.

pick.q: He's in love with her; it's ___.
opts: as plain as the nose on your face
pick.why: Completely obvious = as plain as the nose on your face.

pick.q: The government's new rules on rebates are ___; nobody knows who qualifies.
pick.why: Very confusing = as clear as mud (ironic).

spot.q: After the soufflé collapsed, it was as flat as a crepe.
spot.why: The fixed simile is flat as a pancake.

spot.q: The mechanic replaced the bumper and now the car is as good as fresh.
spot.why: Repaired perfectly = as good as new.

spot.q: The coach looks friendly, but she's as hard as stones.
opts: as hard as a stone heart
spot.why: Tough people are hard as nails.

spot.q: Those sunglasses were as cheap as fries at the market.
spot.why: The British simile keeps chips. North Americans would say dirt cheap.

type.q: The tire was as flat as a ___ by the time we reached the garage.
type.why: As flat as a pancake: completely flat.

type.q: My grandmother survived the war and was as hard as ___.
type.why: As hard as nails: tough. Always plural nails.

type.q: After a new screen, my tablet is as good as ___.
type.why: As good as new: in perfect condition again.

type.q: The answer is as plain as the ___ on your face.
type.why: As plain as the nose on your face: obvious.

type.q: Your explanation of the new tax rules is as clear as ___.
type.why: As clear as mud: ironic, very confusing.

type.q: On the British high street, those T-shirts are as cheap as ___.
type.why: As cheap as chips: very cheap. British.

bank.q: Wrapped in the duvet, the sleeping baby felt ___.
bank.why: Very light = as light as a feather.

bank.q: Wear mitts; the steering wheel will be ___ this morning.
bank.why: Very cold = as cold as ice.

bank.q: Fighting over the TV remote is a family tradition ___.
bank.why: Very old = as old as the hills.

bank.q: From the X-ray it was ___ that the bone was broken.
bank.why: Obvious = as clear as day.

bank.q: Booking the train online is ___ once you have an account.
bank.why: Very easy = as easy as pie.

bank.q: The car battery was ___ after a week at minus thirty.
bank.why: Completely dead = as dead as a doornail.

bank.q: A good night's sleep and I was ___ again.
bank.why: Well again = as right as rain.

bank.q: My uncle in Bristol says his pension fund is ___.
bank.why: Completely secure = as safe as houses (British).

bank.q: The suitcase was light as a ___ on the way there and heavy on the way back.
bank.why: Light as a feather: very light.

bank.q: The vaccine plan is dead as a ___ after the funding cuts.
bank.why: Dead as a doornail: completely finished.

bank.q: Don't worry about the stitches. You'll be as right as ___ soon.
bank.why: As right as rain: fine again.

bank.q: Making bread with this machine is as easy as ___.
bank.why: As easy as pie: very easy.

bank.q: The prairie road was as flat as a ___ for three hundred kilometres.
bank.why: As flat as a pancake: completely flat.

bank.q: The idea of a four-day week is as old as the mountains.
bank.why: The fixed simile is old as the hills.

bank.q: The instructions were as clear like day.
bank.why: As ... as, never as ... like.

bank.q: Our British guide said the old castle walls were as safe as houses.
bank.why: Correct! As safe as houses = completely safe. It sounds British.

bank.q: His shoulders were tense and his handshake was as cold as ice.
bank.why: Correct! Cold as ice can be physical and emotional at once.

bank.a: The old fax machine was as dead as a doornail.
bank.why: The frame: as + adjective + as + noun. Here dead means it no longer works.

bank.a: Setting up the new router was easy as pie.
bank.why: Casual: the first as is dropped.

bank.a: You will be right as rain in a week.
bank.why: Will be + right as rain: a common reassurance.
